content: An asymptomatic carrier, often referred to simply as a carrier, is an individual who is infected with an infectious disease or possesses an abnormal gene associated with a recessive genetic disorder but does not exhibit any symptoms of the condition. Despite not being affected by the disease or disorder themselves, these carriers have the potential to transmit the condition to others. A well-documented historical example of an asymptomatic carrier is Mary Mallon, commonly known as Typhoid Mary. She was an asymptomatic carrier of typhoid fever and worked as a cook for several families in New York City during the early 20th century. Members of these families developed typhoid fever, and investigations by the Health Department traced the source of the infections back to her. It was determined that she harbored the infectious agent without showing any signs of illness herself. Since there was no method to eliminate the disease from her system, efforts were made to prevent her from continuing to work as a cook in order to reduce the risk of further transmission. Another notable example involves the daughters of Queen Victoria, Princess Alice and Princess Beatrix, who were asymptomatic carriers of the X-linked hemophilia gene. Specifically, they carried an abnormal allele of a gene essential for the production of one of the blood clotting factors. Both princesses had children who inherited and subsequently passed on the gene to future generations of the royal families of Spain and Russia, into which they married. Males who inherited the gene developed hemophilia, a condition characterized by impaired blood clotting, while females who carried the gene typically transmitted it to approximately half of their offspring. The genetic term used to describe this type of carrier status for a recessive trait is heterozygote.
